evidence.1.1: Device inventory with ownership, network identifiers and last-seen dates; records reconciling discovered assets to the inventory.
evidence.1.2: Unknown-device records with isolation, removal or authorization decisions and their resolution dates.
evidence.2.1: Installed-software inventory linked to business purpose, ownership and licensing information.
evidence.2.2: Vendor support-status records, software-version inventory and approved unsupported-software exceptions.
evidence.2.3: Unauthorized-installation reports with removal tickets or documented authorization decisions.
evidence.3.1: Data-management process showing accountable owners and handling, retention and disposal responsibilities.
evidence.3.2: Sensitive-data inventory showing locations, owners and records of updates when data or systems change.
evidence.3.3: Data permission exports and access approvals showing how permissions relate to business responsibilities.
evidence.3.4: Retention settings and execution records tied to the organization's documented retention periods.
evidence.3.5: Disposal records showing the affected information or media, disposal method and accountable party.
evidence.3.6: Endpoint encryption coverage and exception reports; configuration records without recovery keys or other secrets.
evidence.4.1: Approved configuration baselines, revision records and deployment or compliance results for scoped assets.
evidence.4.2: Network-device configuration standards, change records and configuration-conformance results.
evidence.4.3: Session-lock policy settings and deployment coverage across the relevant asset types.
evidence.4.4: Server firewall configuration and coverage reports, including documented exceptions.
evidence.4.5: Endpoint firewall policies showing default handling, permitted traffic and deployment coverage.
evidence.4.6: Administrative-access configurations and change records showing secure management channels in use.
evidence.4.7: Default-account inventory and configuration records showing disabled or secured preconfigured accounts.
evidence.5.1: Account inventory with owners, authorization decisions and records of continued-need review.
evidence.5.2: Password-policy settings and credential-handling procedures; never collect actual passwords as Evidence.
evidence.5.3: Account inactivity reports and dated disablement or removal records, with justified exceptions.
evidence.5.4: Privileged-account inventory and account-role assignments showing separation from ordinary user activity.
evidence.6.1: Access requests, recorded approvals and provisioning tickets linked to the granted permissions.
evidence.6.2: Departure or role-change notifications and deprovisioning records showing when access was removed.
evidence.6.3: Externally accessible application inventory and MFA enforcement/exception reports for those applications.
evidence.6.4: Remote-access service configurations and MFA coverage records, including alternative entry paths.
evidence.6.5: Privileged-access inventory and MFA enforcement records for administrative interfaces and accounts.
evidence.7.1: Vulnerability-management procedure identifying scope, responsibilities and the path from detection to resolution.
evidence.7.2: Prioritized remediation backlog, ownership and recorded process-review or exception decisions.
evidence.7.3: Operating-system patch deployment results, failed-update follow-up and excluded-device decisions.
evidence.7.4: Application-update coverage, deployment results and follow-up for failed or unsupported applications.
evidence.8.1: Log-management documentation covering sources, retention, review responsibilities and changes.
evidence.8.2: Audit-source inventory, enabled-event configurations and dated event samples from scoped assets.
evidence.8.3: Logging storage capacity, retention settings and alerts or follow-up for storage shortfalls.
evidence.9.1: Browser/email-client version inventory and support-status review with upgrade or exception records.
evidence.9.2: DNS-filtering configuration and coverage for local and remote endpoints, including bypass exceptions.
evidence.10.1: Endpoint protection inventory, deployment coverage and health reports for relevant systems.
evidence.10.2: Automatic signature-update configuration and reports identifying stale or failed updates.
evidence.10.3: Autorun/autoplay policy configuration and deployment results for supported removable-media endpoints.
evidence.11.1: Recovery documentation identifying scope, priorities, backup responsibilities and protection of recovery data.
evidence.11.2: Backup schedules, job results and follow-up records for failures or missed coverage.
evidence.11.3: Backup access controls and encryption settings appropriate to the original information's sensitivity.
evidence.11.4: Recovery-copy architecture and isolation settings showing separation from primary-system compromise paths.
evidence.12.1: Network infrastructure version/support inventory and upgrade, change or exception records.
evidence.14.1: Awareness-program ownership, current content and workforce assignment/completion records.
evidence.14.2: Social-engineering awareness material and participation or follow-up records for the scoped workforce.
evidence.14.3: Authentication and credential-handling training content and participation records.
evidence.14.4: Data-handling training covering storage, sharing and disposal, with workforce completion records.
evidence.14.5: Accidental-disclosure prevention material and records showing delivery to relevant personnel.
evidence.14.6: Incident-recognition/reporting training and current reporting instructions distributed to personnel.
evidence.14.7: Workforce guidance on recognizing missing updates and records of training or reported update issues.
evidence.14.8: Remote/insecure-network awareness material and participation records for personnel handling enterprise data.
evidence.15.1: Service-provider inventory with service descriptions, classifications and accountable business contacts.
evidence.17.1: Incident leadership and backup-role assignments, with records of role confirmation or exercises.
evidence.17.2: Incident notification contacts and records confirming that contact details remain current.
evidence.17.3: Documented incident-reporting process and workforce communications explaining the reporting path.

1.implementation: Typical implementation connects discovery results to an owned inventory and a decision about authorization. Include remote and intermittently connected devices; track unknown assets through resolution rather than merely listing them.
1.evidence: Asset inventory with owners and last-seen dates; discovery reconciliation; unauthorized-device isolation or approval tickets.

2.implementation: Typical implementation reconciles installed software against an authorized list, identifies unsupported versions and records decisions or removal. A purchased-license list alone may not show what is actually installed.
2.evidence: Software inventory; supported-version checks; approved exception records; removal or upgrade tickets.

3.implementation: Depending on the safeguard, connect the data's sensitivity and owner to its location, allowed access, retention, disposal or encryption. Check that the documented rule covers the actual systems and copies in scope.
3.evidence: Data inventory and handling rules; permission exports; retention settings; disposal records; encryption compliance reports.

4.implementation: Typical implementation uses an approved configuration baseline and verifies that it reaches the relevant devices, servers or network equipment. Record exceptions and failed deployment coverage rather than relying only on a template.
4.evidence: Configuration standard; device configuration export; firewall or session-lock settings; baseline compliance and exception records.

5.implementation: Typical implementation distinguishes ordinary, privileged and service accounts, establishes ownership and verifies continued need. Check inactive accounts and privileged separation in the actual identity systems, not only in a policy.
5.evidence: Account inventory; authorization review records; inactivity reports; privileged-account list; password-policy settings without passwords.

6.implementation: Typical implementation connects approved access to provisioning and timely removal. For MFA safeguards, check the named access channel's coverage, exclusions and enforcement; enrolling some users does not establish complete coverage.
6.evidence: Access requests and approvals; joiner/mover/leaver tickets; deprovisioning records; scoped MFA enforcement and exception reports.

7.implementation: Typical implementation assigns responsibility for vulnerabilities and patching, prioritizes remediation and checks failed or excluded deployments. A scheduled update job alone does not show that in-scope systems received the updates.
7.evidence: Vulnerability and remediation procedures; prioritized backlog; patch deployment results; failure follow-up and exception records.

8.implementation: Typical implementation defines useful events, collects them from the relevant assets and checks retention and storage capacity. Verify missing sources and collection failures, not only whether a logging tool exists.
8.evidence: Logging standard; source inventory; event samples; retention and storage settings; collection failure follow-up.

9.implementation: Typical implementation covers the browsers, email clients or DNS paths used both on-site and remotely. Document unsupported clients or bypass paths and how they are handled.
9.evidence: Browser/email version inventory; support review; DNS filtering configuration and coverage; exception records.

10.implementation: Typical implementation confirms endpoint coverage, current protection settings and update health. For removable-media protections, check actual policy enforcement on the relevant endpoint types.
10.evidence: Endpoint protection coverage and health reports; signature update status; autorun/autoplay configuration; exclusion records.

11.implementation: Typical implementation identifies recovery priorities, verifies backup success and protects recovery copies against the threats affecting primary systems. A successful backup is not itself proof that restoration or isolation has been demonstrated.
11.evidence: Recovery procedure; backup scope and job logs; failure follow-up; backup access/encryption settings; isolation configuration and available restore-test records.

12.implementation: Typical implementation inventories network hardware and software, checks support status and tracks necessary upgrades or justified exceptions. Include network equipment outside the main office.
12.evidence: Network-device inventory; software support review; update/change records; unsupported-device exception decisions.

14.implementation: Typical implementation covers the relevant workforce and topic, tracks participation and follows up on gaps. Content availability alone does not show that people received or understood it; connect the topic to practical reporting and handling procedures.
14.evidence: Training material for this topic; scoped workforce assignment and completion records; follow-up records; reporting instructions.

15.implementation: Typical implementation records the services used, accountable business contacts and relevant classifications. Reconcile the inventory with procurement and business activity so unmanaged providers are visible.
15.evidence: Service-provider inventory; owner and classification fields; procurement reconciliation; supplier review records.

17.implementation: Typical implementation gives personnel a clear reporting path and identifies incident leadership and backup contacts. Verify that contact details and responsibilities remain usable when key staff are unavailable.
17.evidence: Incident roles and contact list; reporting procedure; workforce communications; contact verification or exercise records.
